questions.prompt: The Wolfe conditions on a step length are
options: the requirement that the new gradient be exactly zero
sufficient decrease, plus a curvature test on the new directional derivative
the single requirement that the step length equal \(1\)
the requirement that the Hessian equal the identity
questions.explanation: Sufficient decrease is the Armijo inequality, with parameter \(c_1 \in (0, 1)\). The curvature test asks the new directional derivative to be at least \(c_2\) times the old one, with \(c_1 < c_2 < 1\). A length of \(1\) can fail either test. The Hessian is not required to be the identity. A zero new gradient would be stationarity of the whole problem, which a line search does not demand.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = -t^2\), with start \(t = 1\), direction \(d = 1\), and step length \(1\). The step is \(s = 1\) and the gradient change is \(y\). What is \(y\, s\)?
questions.explanation: The derivative is \(-2t\). It equals \(-2\) at \(t = 1\) and \(-4\) at \(t = 2\). Then \(y = -4 - (-2) = -2\) and \(s = 1\), so \(y s = -2\). The objective falls from \(-1\) to \(-4\), so a pure decrease test can accept the step, but the curvature product is negative. Reporting \(2\) drops the sign of \(y\). Reporting \(-4\) is the new derivative. Reporting \(-6\) adds the derivatives instead of subtracting them.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: If the old directional derivative is negative, the Wolfe curvature test forces the new directional derivative to be
options: at least \(c_2\) times the old one, hence no more negative than that multiple
strictly more negative than the old one
exactly zero
equal to the trace of the Hessian
questions.explanation: The test is \(\nabla f(x+td)^T d \ge c_2 \nabla f(x)^T d\) with \(c_2 < 1\). The old directional derivative is negative, and \(c_2\) times it is a larger number (closer to zero, or beyond). The new directional derivative has to reach at least that value. Asking it to be more negative is the opposite inequality. The test does not require a stationary point, and it does not mention the trace.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: Put this argument that the Wolfe conditions imply \(y^T s > 0\) in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: Curvature compares the new directional derivative with the old one, so the old value and the fact that it is negative have to come first. Subtracting \(g\) uses that inequality and produces the difference that equals \(y^T d\). Multiplying by the positive length \(t\) turns \(y^T d\) into \(y^T s\). The sign of the lower bound uses \(c - 1 < 0\) and \(g < 0\), which are already in the earlier steps. The two comparisons cannot be swapped: the subtraction is the curvature inequality after a rewrite, not a separate test.

steps: Start from a descent direction, so the directional derivative \(g\) is negative, and from a step \(s = t d\) with \(t > 0\).
Apply the curvature inequality: the new directional derivative is at least \(c\) times \(g\), with \(c < 1\).
Subtract \(g\) from both sides, which produces a difference of directional derivatives at least \((c - 1) g\).
Multiply by \(t > 0\) to conclude that \(y^T s\) is at least \(t(c-1)g\), hence positive.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = t^2\), with start \(t = 2\) and direction \(d = -1\). Use \(c_1 = 1/10\) and \(c_2 = 1/2\). Sufficient decrease uses \(c_1\). Curvature requires the new directional derivative to be at least \(c_2\) times the old one. Which step lengths satisfy both?
questions.explanation:
The derivative is \(2t\), so the old directional derivative is \(4 \cdot (-1) = -4\). The new point is \(2 - \alpha\), and the new directional derivative is \(-2(2-\alpha)\).
• At \(\alpha = 1/2\) the new directional derivative is \(-3\), and \(-3 \ge -2\) fails. Sufficient decrease holds, since \(2.25 \le 3.8\), but curvature does not.
• At \(\alpha = 1\) the new directional derivative is \(-2\), so curvature holds with equality. The value \(1\) is at most \(4 - 0.4 = 3.6\), so decrease holds too.
• At \(\alpha = 2\) the new directional derivative is \(0\), which is greater than \(-2\). The value \(0\) is at most \(4 - 0.8 = 3.2\), so both tests hold.
• At \(\alpha = 4\) the new directional derivative is \(4\), so curvature holds, but the value \(4\) is larger than \(4 - 1.6 = 2.4\), so sufficient decrease fails.

questions.prompt: A step length \(t > 0\), a curvature parameter \(c \in (0, 1)\), and a negative directional derivative \(g\) produce the Wolfe lower bound \(t(c-1)g\) on \(y^T s\). That bound equals
questions.explanation: Curvature says the new directional derivative is at least \(c g\). Subtracting \(g\) leaves a difference at least \((c-1)g\). The gradient change along \(s = t d\) multiplies that difference by \(t\), which is \(t(c-1)g\). Every declared name appears. Because \(c-1\) and \(g\) are both negative, the bound is positive. Using \(t(c+1)g\) has the wrong sign and is negative for these ranges. Using \(t c g\) drops the subtraction of the old directional derivative. Using \((c-1)g/t\) divides by the length instead of multiplying.

questions.prompt: A note checks the length \(1/2\) for \(f(t) = t^2\), start \(t = 2\), direction \(d = -1\), \(c_1 = 1/10\), and \(c_2 = 1/2\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The old directional derivative is \(-4\). The point \(2 + (1/2)(-1) = 1.5\) has derivative \(3\), so the new directional derivative is \(-3\). The Armijo right-hand side is \(4 + (1/10)(1/2)(-4) = 3.8\), and \(2.25 \le 3.8\), so sufficient decrease holds. Curvature asks for \(-3 \ge (1/2)(-4) = -2\). That comparison fails. The inequality \(-3 \le -2\) is true as arithmetic and is the wrong direction for the test.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
steps: The new point is \(1.5\), and the new directional derivative is \(3 \cdot (-1) = -3\).
Sufficient decrease holds, because the new value \(2.25\) is at most \(4 - 0.2 = 3.8\).
reasons: Curvature requires the new directional derivative to be at least \(c_2\) times the old one. Here \(-3 < -2\), so the test fails.
The old directional derivative is not \(-4\).
Sufficient decrease fails for these values.

questions.prompt: For \(f(t) = t^2\), start \(t = 2\), direction \(d = -1\), and step length \(1\), what is \(y^T s\)?
questions.explanation: The step is \(s = -1\). The derivative changes from \(4\) at \(t = 2\) to \(2\) at \(t = 1\), so \(y = 2 - 4 = -2\). Then \(y^T s = (-2)(-1) = 2\). Reporting \(-2\) is \(y\), or \(s\), rather than the product. Reporting \(4\) is the old derivative. Reporting \(6\) adds the absolute values of the derivatives.

questions.prompt: The two Wolfe parameters must satisfy
questions.explanation: Sufficient decrease uses a \(c_1\) strictly between \(0\) and \(1\), so the right-hand side still goes down when the directional derivative is negative, but not as fast as the linear model. Curvature uses a larger \(c_2\) that is still strictly less than \(1\). That gap is what makes \(y^T s\) positive. Setting \(c_1 = 1\) asks for a decrease the linear model itself may not beat on a curved function, and \(c_2 = 0\) does not force the slope to rise. A parameter above \(1\), or a negative \(c_1\), leaves the standard pair.

questions.prompt: A positive product \(y^T s\) is the curvature hypothesis used to keep which update positive definite?
options: a power iteration
a projection onto a half-space with no gradient change
the BFGS update of an inverse Hessian approximation
a simplex pivot
questions.explanation: BFGS divides by \(y^T s\) and preserves positive definiteness when that product is positive and the previous approximation was positive definite. The Wolfe curvature test is one way to guarantee the product. A simplex pivot changes a basis. Power iteration multiplies by a fixed matrix. A half-space projection does not form \(y\).

questions.prompt: For \(f(t) = t^2\), start \(t = 2\), and direction \(d = -1\), the curvature test with \(c_2 = 9/10\) holds only when the step length is at least some positive number. What is that number?
questions.explanation: The new directional derivative is \(-4 + 2\alpha\), and the old one is \(-4\). Curvature says \(-4 + 2\alpha \ge (9/10)(-4)\), so \(2\alpha \ge 4 - 3.6 = 0.4\), and \(\alpha \ge 0.2\). Reporting \(0.4\) stops before dividing by \(2\). Reporting \(2\) is the factor in front of \(\alpha\), from the second derivative times the direction. Reporting \(9/10\) is \(c_2\).

questions.prompt: A line search that keeps only sufficient decrease, and skips the curvature test, can return a step with
options: an accepted length of \(0\)
\(y^T s < 0\), which the BFGS positive-definiteness argument excludes
\(y^T s > 0\) for every objective, including \(f(t) = -t^2\)
a zero gradient at the new point, for every objective
questions.explanation: On \(f(t) = -t^2\), the step from \(t = 1\) in the direction \(d = 1\) with length \(1\) decreases the objective from \(-1\) to \(-4\), so a sufficient-decrease test can accept it, while \(y s = -2\). BFGS needs a positive product and does not promise to stay positive definite for this step. The same example shows the product is not positive for every objective. The new derivative is \(-4\), not zero. A length of \(0\) does not move, and the line search looks for a positive length.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.
